task: Content Studio HITL-3 editor persistence and approve-time content promotion
decision: Treat the final-content approval editor as a client-primary draft flow with backend durability. The editor now keeps the latest review markdown in localStorage keyed by company slug + brief id + run id, periodically autosaves that markdown to a dedicated backend draft artifact (`review_draft.md`) every 5 minutes while the draft is dirty, and includes the latest `content_markdown` in approve/send-back/publish API calls. The backend exposes additive `GET/PUT /api/v1/content/v13/{run_id}/draft/content` endpoints and, on final approval, promotes `approval_data.content_markdown` into `final.md` and `ContentPiece.final_markdown` instead of approving the stale pre-edit article body.
rationale: The previous editor was ephemeral: navigating away from the detail view unmounted Tiptap, the page reloaded article content only from the server artifact, and the approve route accepted only `editor_notes`. That meant user edits disappeared on reopen and the approved artifact never reflected the reviewed text. Making the client draft primary preserves fast local editing, while backend autosave plus approve-time promotion gives crash/reload durability and ensures the canonical final artifact matches what the reviewer actually approved.
alternatives: Persist every keystroke directly to the canonical final artifact — rejected because it makes typing latency and accidental partial edits too expensive and blurs the difference between draft and approved content
Keep persistence client-only and rely on the browser cache/localStorage forever — rejected because refreshes across devices/processes and final approve semantics still need a durable server copy
Save only `editor_notes` and ignore edited content on approve — rejected because the approved article would still diverge from the text the reviewer edited in the UI
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. Review cards now restore local edits when reopened, autosave server-side draft content on an interval, and final approval promotes the edited markdown into the canonical final artifact. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/api/test_content_v13.py -k 'ReviewDraftContent or td_content_review_routes_to_durable_resume_queue' -q` (4 passed), `venv/bin/pytest tests/api/test_content_v13.py tests/content_engine/test_pipeline_v13.py -k 'approve_content or ReviewDraftContent or edited_markdown_from_review_state' -q` (7 passed), `venv/bin/pytest tests/content_engine/test_pipeline_v13.py -k edited_markdown_from_review_state -q` (1 passed), `venv/bin/python -m py_compile api/schemas/content_v13.py api/routers/content_v13.py core/content_engine/pipeline_v13.py` (clean), and `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit` (clean).

task: Content Studio detail view should keep topic-assignment descriptions and planner metadata after cards leave Queue
decision: Treat `topic_assignments` as the durable source of planner/topic metadata for DB-backed Content Studio cards linked by `content_pieces.topic_assignment_id`. `DbContentDataService.get_briefs()` now bulk-loads the linked topic assignments and maps buyer stage, intent type, persona, priority factors, estimated word count, citation opportunity, description, target keywords, and content angle back onto each `ContentBriefListItem`, instead of assuming only GA Redis cards need that enrichment.
rationale: The sidebar and Metrics tab were already rendering correctly when `ContentCard` carried planner metadata and `gapContext`, but once a card moved from Queue into `pending_brief_approval` or active CE, the selected card came from the DB-backed `/content/briefs` list payload, which was only returning `content_pieces` fields plus status overrides. That dropped the topic-assignment description and related planner context from the left sidebar. Rehydrating those fields from `topic_assignments` keeps the detail view consistent across Queue, brief review, and active production stages without depending on ephemeral Redis-only card metadata.
alternatives: Persist all planner metadata redundantly into `content_pieces.evaluation_results` and read it only from there — rejected because the authoritative planner/topic-assignment source already exists and the card should survive metadata evolution without duplicating every field

Make the frontend fetch topic-assignment details separately after selecting a card — rejected because the selected card already comes from `/content/briefs`, and splitting this contract across another request would add latency and more state drift in the detail view

Keep the old runtime-only sidebar for active cards — rejected because it duplicated the center-panel pipeline state and hid the topic brief that users need while approving briefs or monitoring generation
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. DB-backed `pending_brief_approval` and active CE cards now keep the same topic-assignment description and planner metadata that Queue cards expose, and the right sidebar continues to use the topic-focused gap context already attached to those cards. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/services/test_db_content_data_backend.py -q` (12 passed) and `venv/bin/python -m py_compile core/services/db_content_data.py tests/services/test_db_content_data_backend.py` (clean).

task: Content Studio right-sidebar structural compliance and E-E-A-T for content review/completed cards
decision: Review and completed article detail views must source structural compliance, citation prediction, and E-E-A-T from the content-engine evaluator snapshot for that exact generated article, not from the site-audit module. `pipeline_v13.py` now persists a rich article-level eval snapshot (`eval_history`, `final_passed`, latest dimension summary, and `cps`) onto the linked `content_piece` before entering `pending_content_approval`, and approved-piece persistence keeps the same payload. `DbContentDataService.get_brief_detail()` returns both `eval_history` and `cps` from `evaluation_results`, which is the contract the frontend adapters already use to render structural compliance and E-E-A-T.
rationale: The blank review sidebar was caused by a timing mismatch: the review UI reads from the DB-backed `content_piece`, but until this fix the pipeline only wrote a thin summary after final approval, so `pending_content_approval` cards still pointed at the early placeholder row with no evaluator history or CPS. Site-audit E-E-A-T is the wrong substitute because it measures page/site quality in a separate pipeline, while the review sidebar needs article-specific scores for the exact generated draft the human is approving.
alternatives: Populate the review sidebar from site-audit scores — rejected because site-audit is page/site-level and can diverge materially from the generated article's evaluator result

Recompute structural compliance and E-E-A-T in the detail API on demand — rejected because the pipeline already has the authoritative evaluator output and recomputation would add latency and drift risk
Wait until final approval to persist evaluator history — rejected because `pending_content_approval` is itself a first-class detail view and must render the metrics before the user approves
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. `pending_content_approval` and completed article detail views now read article-level structural compliance, citation prediction, and E-E-A-T from the content-engine evaluator snapshot stored on the linked `content_piece`. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/content_engine/test_pipeline_v13.py -k 'ContentReview or pending_content_review_persists_eval_snapshot_for_sidebar_metrics' -q` (5 passed), `venv/bin/pytest tests/services/test_db_content_data_backend.py -q` (13 passed), and `venv/bin/python -m py_compile core/content_engine/pipeline_v13.py core/services/db_content_data.py tests/content_engine/test_pipeline_v13.py tests/services/test_db_content_data_backend.py` (clean).

task: Content Planner priority queue visibility after sending topics to Content Engine
decision: Only the Priority Queue section should hide topics once they have been sent to Content Engine. The frontend assignment model now carries backend `status`, the Priority Queue view renders only queueable assignments (`not_started`), and `approveAssignments()` optimistically marks selected rows `approved` so they disappear immediately from Priority Queue while the GA launch runs. Other planner surfaces continue to receive the broader non-rejected assignment set, and pipeline-launch rollback restores the affected rows back to `not_started`.
rationale: The previous planner data path dropped backend assignment status when adapting Topic Discovery assignments, so the Priority Queue could not distinguish unsent topics from already-approved/in-flight ones. As a result, topics remained visible in Priority Queue even after the user sent them to Content Engine. The user only requested this behavior change for the Priority Queue section, not for the rest of Planner, so a queue-only filter at the page/view layer preserves existing explorer behavior while making the priority list reflect actionable items only.
alternatives: Filter all planner surfaces to queueable statuses only — rejected because the request was explicitly scoped to the Priority Queue section
Remove approved topics from the entire local assignment store after send — rejected because rollback and other planner views would lose state they may still need

Require a backend-only filtered endpoint just for Priority Queue — rejected because the existing assignment list already carries status and the queue-only distinction belongs at the UI section boundary
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. Assignments now retain backend `status`, `approveAssignments()` optimistically flips selected rows to `approved`, rollback restores them to `not_started` if pipeline launch fails, and the Priority Queue section renders only `not_started` assignments so sent topics disappear immediately from that list. Validation: `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit`.

task: Content Studio completed/published detail view article rendering
decision: Completed and published Content Studio cards should reuse the final-article renderer rather than falling back to the generic done-state placeholder. `FullPageView` now treats `completed` and `published` as article-bearing states, and `ArticleEditor` supports a read-only mode that disables editing, review comments, and the bottom formatting toolbar while still rendering the full article body.
rationale: The completed-column detail view was blank because the article body branch only ran for `review` and `pending_content_approval`; once a card entered `completed`, the UI switched to a generic placeholder view despite the final article being available. Reusing the same article renderer preserves consistent reading layout and left-sidebar outline behavior while avoiding a separate completed-only article component.
alternatives: Build a second dedicated completed-article viewer — rejected because the existing article renderer already handles the layout and only needed a read-only switch
Keep completed cards on the placeholder done-state screen — rejected because users expect to read the final article from the completed column
Render the review editor unchanged for completed cards — rejected because completed/published detail views should not expose editing/comment controls
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. Completed and published cards now render the final article body in the center panel using `ArticleEditor` read-only mode, and the generic done placeholder is only used for non-article terminal states. Validation: `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit`.

task: Approved content should leave the Content Studio kanban and enter a dedicated Unpublished Pages staging surface in Content Performance
decision: Do not create a second backend staging model. Keep final approval writing the existing `completed` brief/content state, remove terminal approved/published cards from the Content Studio board, and make Content Performance responsible for the unpublished staging list by reusing the existing `/companies/{slug}/content/briefs` endpoint filtered to `status === completed && !published_url`. The only frontend surface that triggers CMS publish is the unpublished staging detail view, which reuses `FullPageView` in read-only mode and calls the existing `POST /api/v1/cms/publish` endpoint.
rationale: The user wants a clear product distinction between approving content quality and publishing to the CMS. That distinction already exists in the backend data: approved-but-unpublished content appears as `completed` with no `published_url`, while published content already flips `content_pieces` to `published` and sets `published_url`/`published_at`. Reusing those fields avoids inventing a second staging lifecycle, keeps publish state single-sourced in the existing CMS path, and lets Content Performance act as the staging inventory for unpublished pages.
alternatives: Add a brand-new backend `staged` / `unpublished` status and separate API surface — rejected because the existing `completed` + `published_url` contract already distinguishes approved-but-unpublished content and keeps the change smaller

Keep the approved column in Content Studio and also mirror approved cards into Content Performance — rejected because it duplicates the same staging inventory across two surfaces and muddies the handoff

Allow publish from both Content Studio review detail and Content Performance unpublished detail — rejected because the product requirement is to separate final approval from CMS publish and make Content Performance the post-approval staging area
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. Content Studio now removes terminal cards from the kanban and no longer exposes publish during `pending_content_approval`. Content Performance now has an `Unpublished Pages` tab backed by the briefs list, and its row detail view reuses the final-article renderer with a real CMS publish action wired to `/api/v1/cms/publish`. Validation: `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit`.

task: Approved-but-unpublished detail view SEO metadata persistence and CMS publish handoff
decision: Persist the detail-view SEO/publish sidebar state under `content_pieces.evaluation_results.publish_metadata` for this slice instead of adding a new dedicated column/table. The content briefs API now surfaces that payload with defaults, the shared `FullPageView` autosaves edits through a new content-data endpoint, and the CMS publish route consumes the same payload so the sidebar is the single source of truth for slug/meta fields at publish time.
rationale: The product gap was real but the fastest safe path did not require a schema migration. `content_pieces` already has a durable JSONB field (`evaluation_results`) attached to the exact approved/published artifact we need, and that field is already the source of truth for other post-generation sidebar data such as evaluator output and gap context. Using a nested `publish_metadata` object there let us add a durable API contract, frontend autosave, and publish-time metadata handoff immediately without waiting on database rollout. A later cleanup can move this payload into a dedicated publish-metadata column if the shape grows or cross-system querying becomes important.
alternatives: Add a new `publish_metadata_json` or dedicated SEO columns on `content_pieces` now — rejected for this slice because it would require a DB migration before the user could use the flow locally
Keep the SEO sidebar as pure client state and only send it during publish — rejected because the user explicitly needs the fields connected to the backend and preserved before the publish click
Store the SEO payload on `content_engine_topic_runs.metadata_json` — rejected because publish state belongs to the durable content piece and should work for non-TD content paths too
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. The detail view now hydrates SEO metadata from the backend, autosaves edits, and passes the same payload into CMS publish. The publish route and service were also extended so successful CMS publish immediately registers the page into Content Inventory, which makes the card leave the Unpublished Pages list without waiting for a later CMS sync. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/services/test_db_content_data_backend.py tests/api/test_cms.py tests/services/test_cms_service.py -q`, `venv/bin/pytest tests/api/test_content_data.py -q`, `venv/bin/pytest tests/cms/test_wordpress_adapter.py -q`, and `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit`.

task: Content Performance Pages visibility immediately after CMS publish/sync
decision: Treat CMS publish, CMS refresh, and CMS sync as inventory-changing operations that must invalidate the GA4/content-performance cache family (`cache:ga4:{company_slug}:*`) in addition to the CMS cache family. The publish/refresh routers now invalidate GA4 caches after successful writes, and `run_cms_sync_task()` invalidates GA4 caches in its terminal cleanup path after sync commits.
rationale: Live diagnosis on `webflow` showed the content was successfully published and present in `content_inventory`, but the Pages tab still rendered the old 2-page snapshot because Content Performance table/velocity responses are cached by company and lookback window, while the CMS flows only invalidated `cache:cms:*`. A user-visible Pages surface that is backed by `content_inventory` cannot wait for an unrelated GA4 cache TTL after the CMS mutates that inventory. Cache invalidation belongs in the CMS write paths that cause the inventory change.
alternatives: Rely on the 5-10 minute GA4 cache TTL to self-heal — rejected because it makes successful publish look broken and forces the user to guess when the UI will catch up
Invalidate caches only from the frontend after publish — rejected because CMS sync runs in the backend task runner too, and cache ownership belongs server-side
Remove Content Performance caching entirely — rejected because the cached table/velocity responses are still useful once invalidation semantics are correct
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. Publish/refresh now invalidate GA4/content-performance caches immediately, and CMS sync does the same after completion. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/api/test_cms.py tests/api/test_cms_sync_prompt_chain.py -q` (65 passed, 1 pre-existing warning).

task: Per-page drawer enrichment for Content Studio pages published through CMS
decision: Treat CMS publish for Content Studio output as an enrichment point, not just a URL-registration event. `ContentInventoryService.register_published_content()` now accepts rendered HTML plus publish metadata and reuses the gap-analysis S4 structural extractor (`compute_structural_signals`) to populate `content_inventory.structural_signals` with the full rich signal payload at publish time. The same publish path also persists `published_at`, SEO summary fields, and best-effort auto-generates content-to-prompt links for the new inventory row via the standard Content-to-Prompt orchestrator.
rationale: The per-page drawer was empty for newly published Content Studio pages because CMS publish only inserted a thin inventory row. Structural compliance depended on `content_inventory.structural_signals`, citation timeline depended on prompt links, and the drawer header depended on inventory `published_at`, but none of those fields were produced until some unrelated later pipeline run, if ever. Reusing the exact S4 extractor keeps structural semantics aligned with Gap Analysis instead of inventing a second, shallower signal model for published pages.
alternatives: Keep publish-time inventory registration thin and wait for a later CMS sync or site-audit crawl to enrich the page — rejected because the drawer remains effectively empty right after publish
Implement a separate lightweight HTML parser just for Content Performance — rejected because it would drift from the established S4 structural-signal contract
Only store a subset of legacy structural columns at publish time — rejected because the user explicitly asked for structural detail at least as rich as the S4 gap-analysis output
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. New CMS-published Content Studio pages now land in inventory with S4-derived structural signals and publish metadata immediately, and prompt generation is triggered from the publish path instead of only from CMS sync's `new_page_ids` branch. Query Coverage in the drawer now reads the real backend field. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/services/test_content_inventory_service.py tests/services/test_cms_service.py -q`, `venv/bin/pytest tests/api/test_cms.py tests/api/test_content_performance.py -q`, and `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit`.

task: Per-page Content Performance drawer platform semantics and header ownership
decision: The per-page drawer should treat citation-platform coverage and GA4 AI-referral sessions as distinct signals. Backend detail responses now expose `published_at` directly, and the frontend Platform Distribution section merges `platforms` boolean citation presence with `ai_platform_breakdown` session counts instead of treating GA4 sessions as a proxy for being cited on that AI platform. Drawer fetch failures are also surfaced explicitly instead of silently collapsing into the same no-data copy.
rationale: The previous Platform Distribution UI encoded the wrong product meaning: if Daily Tracker said a page was cited by ChatGPT but GA4 had zero AI referral sessions, the card still appeared empty. Conversely, a handful of AI sessions from ChatGPT looked like citation-platform presence even when Daily Tracker had no evidence of citation coverage. The header had a similar contract smell because it depended on the table row's publish date rather than the detail endpoint. The drawer should be self-describing and semantically honest about what signal came from where.
alternatives: Keep using only `ai_platform_breakdown` and rename the section to AI referrals — rejected because the backend already has citation-platform booleans and the drawer would still hide a meaningful signal
Replace the section with citation platforms only and drop GA4 sessions — rejected because the referral-session signal is still useful and should not be discarded
Leave the header on table-row `publishedAt` — rejected because detail views should prefer backend-owned detail state when available
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. `published_at` is now part of the detail contract, the drawer header prefers that field, Platform Distribution shows citation presence and GA4 AI-referral sessions separately on each platform card, and detail-load failures render an explicit warning banner. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/services/test_content_performance_service.py tests/api/test_content_performance.py -q` and `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit`.

task: Per-page drawer freshness semantics
decision: Freshness in the Content Performance drawer should be backend-owned and explicitly incomplete when benchmark data is unavailable. The detail endpoint now returns a nested `freshness` object with observed page ages (`content_age_days`, `last_updated_age_days`) and null benchmark fields for cited exemplar ages / score until that data source is wired. The frontend must not synthesize exemplar ages or freshness scores from `freshness_days`.
rationale: The previous drawer multiplied `freshnessDays` by `0.56` and derived a score locally, which created fake precision for the most decision-driving freshness comparison on the page. That metric was not auditable and could not be explained from backend evidence. Phase 1 makes the contract honest by exposing only the page dates we actually know and returning `freshness_status='insufficient_data'` until competitive benchmark dates are available.
alternatives: Keep the existing frontend heuristic until exemplar-date data is ready — rejected because it continues to present fabricated benchmark math as a real metric
Hide the freshness section entirely until phase 2 — rejected because observed page age is still useful and can be shown honestly without inventing the benchmark
Compute a backend score anyway from the same heuristic — rejected because moving fake math to the backend would not make it more truthful
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. The drawer now displays backend-owned freshness fields and an explicit insufficient-data explanation instead of a synthetic benchmark and score. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/services/test_content_performance_service.py tests/api/test_content_performance.py -q` and `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit`.

task: Per-page drawer freshness benchmark source and scoring
decision: Content Performance freshness benchmarks should come from gap-analysis cited exemplars, not from frontend heuristics or generic crawl timestamps. Gap-analysis S4 now parses `published_at` / `modified_at` from cited HTML using the existing site-audit freshness extractors, persists those dates into `url_enrichment_cache`, and `ContentPerformanceService` benchmarks each published page against the cited exemplar median age using `modified_at` preferentially and `published_at` as a fallback. When no exemplar dates exist but the page itself has usable dates, the backend now falls back to an explicit simple age-band heuristic (`heuristic_fresh`, `heuristic_recent`, `heuristic_stale`, `heuristic_old`) instead of returning null score/state. The backend owns benchmark sample size, avg/median ages, delta-vs-benchmark, status, and freshness score.
rationale: The drawer needs a defensible comparative freshness metric, and the best available comparison set is the exemplar URLs already chosen by gap analysis for the targeted page's open query gaps. Persisting exemplar dates at S4 keeps the benchmark aligned with the rest of the gap-analysis evidence model and avoids inventing a second enrichment pipeline just for Content Performance. Using `modified_at` before `published_at` matches how freshness should behave for living documents that are updated over time.
alternatives: Continue returning only observed page ages until a generic crawl-date source exists — rejected because it leaves the comparative benchmark undefined even though the cited exemplar set already exists

Use Daily Tracker citations as the primary freshness benchmark source — rejected for now because the relevant exemplar publish/modified dates are already closer to gap-analysis persistence and do not require a second evidence extraction path
Benchmark against exemplar average age only — rejected because median is more robust to outlier pages with extremely old or extremely fresh dates
outcome: Implemented on 2026-04-11. The drawer freshness payload now becomes benchmarked when cited exemplar dates exist, falls back to an explicit age-based heuristic when only the page's own dates are available, and still returns `insufficient_data` only when published/modified dates are missing entirely. Validation: `venv/bin/pytest tests/services/test_content_performance_service.py tests/api/test_content_performance.py -q` (82 passed, then targeted heuristic regression tests passed) and `venv/bin/pytest tests/gap_analysis/test_persistence.py tests/gap_analysis/steps/test_s4_enrich_citations.py -q` (77 passed, 1 pre-existing warning).
